title: Verifier‑Assisted versus One‑Shot LLM Intent→Configuration: A Paired NetOpsTraceBench Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed NetOpsTraceBench, a paired comparison of a one‑shot NL→configuration pipeline and a verifier‑assisted generate–validate–repair pipeline on 1,200 intent→config episodes (1,199 complete pairs) using gpt-5-mini, a deterministic NetOps validator, and Mininet‑style emulation. The preregistered binary episode success required (a) validator acceptance of the final config, (b) no emulator availability degradation above the tolerance, and (c) no automatic rollback. Observed outcomes: baseline successes = 1,196/1,199 (0.9974979149), guarded successes = 1,199/1,199 (1.0000000000), paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0025020851; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25; 95% paired bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0000, 0.0058381985] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Repair was invoked only three times. The preregistered per‑topology confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed or archived; the confirmatory analysis is pooled and documented in archived artifacts (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv). Under the chosen synthetic corpus and validator settings, near‑ceiling baseline performance constrained headroom for measurable verifier gains. All artifacts, seeds, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code are archived to permit reproducible follow‑up sensitivity studies.

sections.introduction:
Generative LLMs are increasingly proposed as components in NetOps pipelines that translate operator intent (natural language) into executable device configurations. Prior surveys and system papers emphasize that operational reliability is a property of the orchestration stack (LLM + verifier + provenance + sandboxed execution) rather than of the base LLM alone [1,2]. Generate–validate–repair (verifier‑assisted) architectures are widely suggested to reduce syntactic and semantic errors in executable outputs, yet reproducible, preregistered, paired evidence that measures whether verifier assistance yields operationally meaningful improvement—using emulator‑grounded rollback‑aware endpoints—is limited.

We therefore preregistered NetOpsTraceBench (study_id = rX4f7-1) to ask: can a reproducible, workflow‑centered paired benchmark (one‑shot vs verifier‑assisted) produce an objective binary success metric that distinguishes verifier assistance from one‑shot generation under controlled emulation? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experimental design and archived execution artifacts; (2) an analysis of 1,199 completed paired episodes using the requested model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic validator; and (3) transparent reporting of an analytic deviation (binary outcomes analyzed via exact McNemar plus bootstrap CI) and an explicit correction requested by peer review: the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed and is not present in the archived confirmatory analysis artifacts. We document that omission here and point readers to the pooled confirmatory artifacts.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and system papers frame LLMs as elements inside broader AIOps/NetOps workflows and repeatedly argue for workflow‑centered evaluation that records generator traces, verifier interactions, and emulator execution to capture operational side effects and rollback risk [1–4]. Concrete verifier‑assisted approaches exist in adjacent domains (NL→formal specs, topology compilation, misconfiguration detection) and show that generator+verifier loops can reduce some classes of errors when verifier rules are representative and task difficulty is controlled [5–10].

Empirical studies document LLM failure modes relevant to NetOps—hallucination, unit/semantic errors, overconfidence/miscalibration, and prompt‑injection susceptibility—which motivate external validators and provenance linkers [11–14]. However, many demonstrations use constructed datasets and domain‑specific validators, leaving open questions about external validity and the operational value of verifier scaffolding across diverse task distributions. NetOpsTraceBench operationalizes recommended practices (preregistration, deterministic task generation, explicit failure rules, emulator checks) to make these dependencies observable and reproducible.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and primary estimand: We preregistered study rX4f7-1 and froze the confirmatory plan (preregistration SHA‑256 = 77abe8b4...). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the preregistration specified inclusion/exclusion rules, contamination thresholds, seeds, stopping rules, and a power plan targeting an absolute 5 percentage‑point increase (MDE = 0.05) at α=0.05 and power = 0.8 under baseline≈0.70 assumptions.

Task corpus, topology clusters, and contamination: The benchmark scope defined 1,200 deterministic tasks split into two simulated topology clusters (edge=600, core=600). Tasks were produced by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with frozen per‑task seeds. Contamination checks (token/subsequence overlap threshold T_contam = 0.85; optional embedding similarity threshold = 0.92) were preregistered; flagged pairs would be excluded automatically. In execution no contamination exclusions occurred (analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty).

Paired pipeline design and shared candidate semantics: For each task we produced a single shared_initial_candidate (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate") that both conditions observed; baseline recorded that candidate without invoking repair, while the guarded pipeline presented the same candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and invoked at most one repair call if the validator rejected the candidate. The shared_initial_candidate design isolates verifier/repair effects by holding generation variability constant across paired episodes. This choice was intentional to attribute any improvement to the verifier/repair stage rather than to independent generation variability, but it also reduces opportunities for divergent outputs and consequently reduces observed repair frequency when initial candidates already satisfy intent constraints.

Validation, emulator checks, and binary success rule: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 performs canonical parsing, enforces workflow_policies from the task payload (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), and outputs validation_after.valid and structured diagnostics. The preregistered episode success rule required: (1) validator acceptance of the final configuration, (2) emulator execution showing no availability degradation above tolerance, and (3) no automatic rollback during simulated execution. Validator and emulator artifacts were recorded per episode.

Analysis plan and documented analytic deviation: The preregistration specified a paired nonparametric test and bootstrap CI computation. Given binary outcomes concentrated in concordant cells, the archived confirmatory analysis executed an exact McNemar two‑sided test and computed a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (bootstrap_seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples). This analytic choice is documented in archived analysis artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/results.json, analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Peer review requested explicit correction regarding per‑cluster analysis (H3); as described in Results below, the preregistered per‑topology confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed and no per‑cluster contingency tables or inferential artifacts were archived for the confirmatory analysis. The pooled confirmatory artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv) contain only the overall counts used for the exact McNemar and bootstrap CI.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed 2,398 of 2,400 planned episodes, producing 1,199 complete pairs (complete_pair_count = 1,199; failed_episode_count = 2). Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1,203 (completed = 1,202; failed = 1) and stage_counts: shared_initial_generation = 1,200, repair = 3, indicating repair was invoked in three episodes only (execution/execution_manifest.json; deterministic_reconciliation.json).

Primary confirmatory outcomes (pooled): The pooled 2×2 contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 1,196, n10 = 3, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Baseline_success_count = 1,196/1,199 = 0.9974979149291076; guarded_success_count = 1,199/1,199 = 1.0. Observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002502085070892446. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0000, 0.005838198498748957] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000), archived in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl and analysis/results.json.

Preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3): The preregistration included a confirmatory subgroup plan (H3) to examine consistency across edge and core topology clusters. Peer review identified and requested correction: the confirmatory analysis executed and archived only pooled inferential results. No per‑cluster McNemar tests or per‑cluster contingency table artifacts were produced for the confirmatory analysis; archived confirmatory files (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json) contain pooled counts only. We therefore report that H3 was not executed as a confirmatory subgroup test and remains unexecuted in the archived confirmatory artifacts. This disclosure is the correction requested by peer review and is supported by the archived artifact set.

Missingness, repair diagnostics, and representative traces: Missingness summary (analysis/missingness_summary.csv) reports complete_pairs = 1,199; failed_baseline_episodes = 1; failed_guarded_episodes = 1; both_missing_pairs = 1. Representative per‑episode scoring artifacts (execution/scoring/task-00000X-*.json) demonstrate that for most tasks validation_after.valid == true and repair_applied == false; repair traces exist for exactly three episodes, matching the repair count in provider audit. Representative artifacts and the full hash manifest permit exact reproduction of these counts.
sections.discussion:
Statistical and operational interpretation: The pooled confirmatory inference shows no statistically significant advantage for the guarded pipeline under the chosen corpus and validator settings (p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Two artifact‑grounded operational explanations are evident. First, near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%) left little headroom: the preregistered MDE (5 pp) was substantially larger than the observed ≈0.25 pp improvement, so the run was underpowered to detect such a small absolute effect under the preregistered assumptions. The archived contingency counts (n10 = 3, n01 = 0) and the bootstrap CI quantify this limitation. Second, task-generator and validator design materially affected repair frequency: deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 produced synthetic tasks with explicit required sequences and the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 accepted the majority of initial candidates, explaining why repair was rarely invoked (repair = 3). The shared_initial_candidate design further constrained generation variability and therefore reduced observable divergence between paired episodes.

Implications of the unexecuted H3: Because the preregistered topology‑cluster breakdown (H3) was not executed for the confirmatory analysis, we cannot draw confirmatory inferences about cross‑cluster consistency from these artifacts. The absence of per‑cluster confirmatory artifacts is archived and reported above; future work using the same archived inputs and seeds could execute per‑cluster analyses as exploratory sensitivity checks, but doing so would constitute additional analysis beyond the archived confirmatory execution and is not part of this report.

Threats to validity and externality: Internal validity is strong for deterministic components (frozen seeds, automated exclusion rules). Construct validity depends on whether the binary success rule maps to operational correctness in production. External validity is limited by: a single requested model family (gpt-5-mini), synthetic/consented tasks, Mininet‑style emulation, and a single deterministic validator configuration. Different verifier strictness, more ambiguous/adversarial tasks, or multiple model families could change repair invocation rates and measured gains. The preregistered analytic deviation (Wilcoxon → exact McNemar) is documented and archived.

Operational recommendations: To evaluate verifier value practically, benchmarks should (a) increase task ambiguity/adversarial content to create headroom for repair, (b) vary verifier strictness to observe repair‑trigger sensitivity, and (c) exercise multiple LLM families and vendor renderers. The archived artifacts here provide reproducible inputs and seeds to support such sensitivity studies.
sections.conclusion: NetOpsTraceBench produced a preregistered, artifact‑rich, paired comparison of one‑shot and verifier‑assisted NL→config pipelines on 1,199 complete pairs. Under the synthetic corpus, deterministic validator settings, and the requested model gpt-5-mini, one‑shot baseline success was near ceiling (≈99.75%); the guarded pipeline increased absolute success by ≈0.25 percentage points (paired difference = 0.0025020851) but this small discordant count (n10 = 3) did not yield statistical significance (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.25; 95% CI includes zero). Peer review correctly identified that the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed; we disclose that omission and point to the pooled confirmatory artifacts (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/results.json). The evidence supports the interpretation that, for this corpus and validator configuration, initial LLM outputs frequently satisfied deterministic intent constraints and therefore repair was rarely exercised; it does not imply that verifiers are never useful. All run artifacts, seeds, provider traces, validator traces, and analysis code are archived to enable exact reproduction and follow‑up sensitivity studies that vary corpus difficulty, verifier strictness, and model family.

limitations: Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini); results do not imply generality across other LLMs or fine‑tuned variants.
Task corpus skew: synthetic/consented tasks yielded near‑ceiling baseline success (≈99.75%), limiting headroom and statistical power to detect practical improvements by guarded pipelines.

Emulator fidelity: Mininet‑style emulation and deterministic validators approximate production behavior but may not capture routing convergence, vendor idiosyncrasies, and other deployment failure modes.

Verifier configuration dependence: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 acceptance thresholds and parsing rules materially affect outcomes; different verifier strictness could change repair invocation rates and measured gains.

Analytic deviation documented: the preregistration specified a Wilcoxon signed‑rank paired procedure; the archived confirmatory analysis used an exact McNemar test because outcomes were binary; this deviation is recorded in archived analysis artifacts.

Unexecuted preregistered subgroup: the preregistered topology‑cluster confirmatory breakdown (H3) was not executed or archived for the confirmatory analysis; no per‑cluster confirmatory contingency tables or inferential outputs exist in the archived confirmatory artifacts.
